description:
The single fixture inventory for contracts/auth/v1/jsonschema/principal.v1.schema.json, read by the Go, Python and TypeScript golden runners. ONE manifest, ONE fixture directory, three runners -- three copies of one corpus is the drift G-70 exists to catch, so a runner that maintains its own list is a review defect.

`accept` is a positive control corpus carrying equal weight to `reject`: a validator that is too strict passes every rejection test while breaking every real caller, and that failure is invisible to a suite asserting only rejections.

Every identifier is unmistakably synthetic per G-73 (fixed EXAMPLE bodies, zero-padded counters, no plausible entropy) and the corpus is swept by a scanner rather than trusted to care -- G-16 forbids a credential value in any golden fixture, and these repos are public.
format_assertion_note: Two different things, do not conflate them. (1) CROSS-LANGUAGE FLOOR: every constraint a reject fixture asserts must use a keyword all three validators enforce -- in practice `pattern`, never `format`, because github.com/google/jsonschema-go records `format` and ignores it during validation (its doc.go, "Deviations from the specification"). (2) DEFENCE IN DEPTH where available: the Python and TypeScript runners MUST still enable format assertion (Python: Draft202012Validator(format_checker=...), which needs rfc3339-validator installed or it silently registers no date-time checker; TypeScript: ajv-formats) and MUST FAIL rather than skip if they cannot -- a format check that silently checks nothing while exiting 0 is the defect this contract exists to prevent.
regex_dialect_note: Every `pattern` here stays inside the common subset of Go RE2, ECMA-262 and Python `re`. RE2 has no back-references and no lookaround, and `\d`/`\w`/`\s` are Unicode in Python and ASCII in the other two. Guarded by a test with positive and negative controls, not by review.

reject.why: ACP-ADR-03 bounds a delegated session at 15 minutes and G-52 requires it revocable and shorter than the base session; a delegation with no expiry is an unbounded one.
actor_chain is REQUIRED and explicitly empty when absent, so a deserializer defaulting a missing array to nil cannot make 'absent' read as 'not delegated'.
Same cross-language floor as expires_at, asserted on a NESTED field -- a walker or a validator that only enforced the top level would pass this.
G-27: a single-segment action is the `is_admin` shape, made unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged.
G-13 requires an exact audience to be pinned; an absent audience is the fail-open case, because an empty expected audience disables the check in at least one JWT library.

ACP-ADR-07 decision 2, G-14 and TRD section 8's own rule ("Grants and entitlements are not identity claims"): entitlement is an input to a decision and never a claim in a credential. This fixture is the executable form of that rule.
Revisions are monotonic and non-negative.

The enforced keyword is `pattern`, not `format`: github.com/google/jsonschema-go records `format` and ignores it during validation, so a fixture asserting `format` would be checked in Python and TypeScript and vacuous in Go.

REGRESSION GUARD for a MEASURED divergence. With the digit class spelled \d this exact document was ACCEPTED by the Python validator and REJECTED by the Go one: Python's `re` treats \d as Unicode and matches Devanagari digits, Go RE2 and ECMA-262 treat it as ASCII. Every digit class is now [0-9], and this fixture is what stops \d being reintroduced -- under \d it turns green in one language and stays red in another.
G-31 requires an allow-cache key to bind grant revision. A principal missing it lets a consumer build a cache key that a grant bump cannot invalidate.

TRD section 3 and G-23: platform-admin authority moves to a separate platform role/action namespace resolved against current state. A superuser bit in a principal is the mechanism being migrated away from, not a field to preserve.
Empty string is not null. Python treats "" as falsy where Go nil-checks a pointer, so a contract accepting "" would mean two different things in two runtimes.

TRD section 11 and G-14 forbid embedding a complete mutable permission set in a credential. The first draft of this schema carried `permissions` copied from the legacy envelope; this fixture is what stops it coming back.

REGRESSION GUARD for a MEASURED divergence, the third in the same family. Python's `re` treats `$` as matching at end-of-string OR immediately before a single trailing newline; Go RE2 and ECMA-262 match only at true end. Executed on all three engines with this exact document: Python ACCEPTED, Go rejected, Node (which is what ajv implements) returned false -- Python the sole outlier, 1 of 3, exactly as with the Unicode \d divergence. No portable pattern fixes it (\Z is Python-only, \z is RE2-only, ECMA-262 has neither), so the Python validator rewrites a trailing `$` to `\Z` and this fixture is what proves that rewrite is installed and working.

TRD section 8 rule 1 / G-20: the authorization subject is the stable principal id, not the user record id. Using a subject id where a principal id belongs is the confusion the two separate fields exist to prevent, so the prefix makes it detectable.
ACP-ADR-05 decision 4 / G-27: an explicit action at the call site, never a broad role check as the final decision.
A relying party must reject an unrecognised contract version rather than parse optimistically. TRD section 21: breaking semantics require v2, and a v2 document is not a v1 document.
Scopes are colon-separated and actions are dotted, deliberately different shapes so the two vocabularies cannot be confused at a call site (G-5: authentication is not authorization).

A delegation of exactly 15 minutes plus 500ns, expressed with ten fractional digits. Before the cap, Python TRUNCATED it to 15 minutes and ACCEPTED it against the ACP-ADR-03 bound while Go saw 15m0.0000005s and refused the identical document -- a bound bypass in one client and a split between both. Python's datetime holds microseconds and Go's time.Time holds nanoseconds, so any timestamp past six fractional digits means different instants in the two runtimes. The schema now caps the fraction at six digits, which all three validators enforce identically, and this fixture is what stops the cap being widened back: it is a REJECT rather than a client-enforced case precisely because the cap removed the surface instead of teaching each client to compare at a precision one of them cannot represent.

`amr` values are the RFC 8176 subset this platform can produce. Federated sign-in is identified by the credential class and the upstream identity, not by an amr value -- and `saml` is not a registered amr name.
NIST SP 800-63B defines aal1-aal3. An unrecognised assurance must deny, not compare greater-than by string order.
ACP-ADR-05 decision 1 / G-26: unknown denies. A class absent from both the Wave 0 frozen 30 and the documented Wave 1 additions is not a compatibility convenience.
The taxonomy is the Wave 0 closed vocabulary; unknown denies.

client_enforced_note: Some rules the contract states cannot be expressed in JSON Schema at all, and the honest place for them is a THIRD fixture category rather than a silence. A duration bound is the clear case: ACP-ADR-03 fixes a delegated session at 15 minutes and G-52 requires it shorter than the base session, but JSON Schema cannot subtract two timestamps, so requiring an `expires_at` FIELD is not a duration BOUND. Fixtures listed here MUST validate against the schema and MUST be refused by every language client. They are what stops the gap being closed by a comment: codex round 1 found this by constructing exactly such a document, and an inventory with only accept/reject had nowhere to put the answer.

reject_by_client.why: A 30-minute delegated session (hop 23:15Z -> 23:45Z). Schema-valid: every timestamp is well formed and expires_at is present. ACP-ADR-03 bounds a delegated session at 15 minutes and G-52 requires it strictly shorter than the base session, so every client must refuse it. Executed before the fix: violations [] and effective_deadline 23:45Z, i.e. accepted end to end.

started_at 23:31Z is AFTER expires_at 23:30Z. Schema-valid for the same reason, and a negative duration trivially satisfies any maximum -- so a bound checked as `expires_at - started_at <= 15m` without also checking the sign accepts it. The ordering check and the duration check are two rules, and this fixture is the one that notices when only the second is implemented.

The canonical two-hop chain, reversed. Schema-valid: every hop is individually well formed and within its own 15-minute bound. But the chain is append-only (TRD section 8 rule 4) and both clients read index zero as the ORIGINATING actor, so a reversed chain reports the later delegator as the real actor -- G-49 requires the real actor to survive downstream, and it does not survive being silently relabelled. Executed before the fix: violations [] and real_actor = ...0003 instead of ...0002, in BOTH languages.

Hop 1 expires at 23:31Z, after hop 0's 23:30Z. Schema-valid and each hop is individually under the 15-minute bound, so the per-hop checks pass; the chain as a whole is still unbounded, because a sub-delegation that outlives the delegation it descends from is not bounded by it (G-52). The ordering rule and the per-hop rule catch different things and this fixture is the one that notices when only the per-hop rule exists.

A revision of exactly 2^53 in DECIMAL form. Schema-valid, because draft 2020-12 defines an integer as any number with a zero fractional part -- and refused by every client, because 2^53+1 rounds down to this same double and a float64 cannot say which of the two arrived. It is a `reject_by_client` case rather than a `reject` one for exactly the reason that category exists: the rule is not expressible in JSON Schema, which has no way to constrain a number's REPRESENTATION.

This fixture exists because the Python half of the guard was unpinned. Deleting the guard outright, or weakening `>=` to `>`, left pytest green while Go went red -- the Go table asserted the boundary and never executed Python, so the language that originally lost the precision was the one with no coverage. Found by lane-auth-wave1's executed read.

A revision of 2^53+1 in decimal form, written as RAW TEXT because a JSON writer destroys it: json.dumps(float(9007199254740993)) emits 9007199254740992.0, so the generator that builds this corpus cannot express the value the fixture is about. That is the same precision loss the guard defends against, occurring one layer up in the tooling -- which is why this file is written literally and must not be regenerated by round-tripping it through a parser.
